entry.title: Watch for El Nino's delayed fallout
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Watch for El Nino's delayed falloutWatch for El Nino's delayed fallout

Modest decline in sown area masks risks to crop yields and rural incomes

premium

El Niño and deficient monsoon rainfall threaten kharif yields, rural incomes and India’s economic growth in the second half of FY27

Nikhil Gupta6 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTDespite a super El Nino and a 12.6 per cent rainfall deficit during the recently concluded Southwest monsoon, the area sown under food grains and oilseeds in the 2026 kharif season declined by just 1.2 per cent year-on-year (YoY). In fact, the area sown remained about 2 per cent above normal. Does this suggest that the adverse economic impact of El Nino will be muted this year? Some market participants certainly seem to think so. I beg to differ, however, for good reason.  It is important to note that the area sown during the kharif season doesn’t change much year-on-year. Based on data for the past 26 years (2000-2025), the average fall in kharif area sown during rainfall-deficit years (about -10 per cent or worse) was only 0.9 per cent. There were eight such years in the period: FY01, FY03, FY05, FY10, FY15, FY16, FY19 and FY24. During moderate or strong El Nino years (only four episodes in FY03, FY10, FY16 and FY24), kharif area sown was down by an average of 1.9 per cent. The average growth in kharif area sown was under 1 per cent during normal (non-El Nino or non-rainfall-deficit) years. The fall of 1.2 per cent in 2026, therefore, is not out of line.  Notwithstanding a small fall in area sown, kharif yield declined by an average of 6.5 per cent during rainfall-deficit years and as much as 8.4 per cent per annum during El Nino years. In contrast, the yield under kharif season grew by 4-6 per cent per annum during normal years. Because of lower yield (due to low water supply and/or higher temperature), the agricultural output under kharif season fell by about 7 per cent annually during rainfall deficit years and as much as 10 per cent per annum during El Nino episodes. This compares with an average growth of 5-7 per cent during normal years.  Not surprisingly, then, real agricultural gross value added (GVA) witnessed an average decline of 0.3 per cent per annum during rainfall-deficit years, with the fall rising to about 1 per cent during El Nino years. During normal years, real agricultural GVA growth averaged 4-5 per cent. Most interestingly, the adverse impact on the real agricultural GVA during El Nino or rainfall-deficit years was entirely concentrated in the second half of the year (2H). For instance, while average growth in the first half of rainfall-deficit years was 2 per cent (and 1 per cent during El Nino years), real agricultural GVA declined by about 2 per cent per annum during the affected period. In the first quarter of 2026-27 (1QFY27), real agricultural GVA grew 3.6 per cent Y-o-Y; however, as yields get adversely affected, we expect it to soften towards 2 per cent Y-o-Y in Q2, before easing to 0.4 per cent in 2HFY27 (not a decline). This will mean a growth of 1.4 per cent in FY27 vs 3 per cent in FY26.  Not only real agricultural GVA but rural income (or wage growth) also gets adversely affected. Based on monthly data available from the Labour Bureau, real rural wage growth was 0.5 per cent per annum during the rainfall-deficit years (and 0.9 per cent annually during El Nino years), only about a quarter of the 1.8 per cent per annum growth during normal years.  Unsurprisingly, the adverse impact was more pronounced in agricultural wages (only about a fifth of the normal-period average) than non-agricultural wages (about half of the normal-period average). In the first five months of FY27 (April-August), real rural wage growth averaged 0.6 per cent Y-o-Y, with only 0.3 per cent growth in agricultural activities and 0.9 per cent growth in non-agricultural activities.  Further, real private final consumption expenditure has also seen slower growth in the affected years — an average growth of 5.5 per cent per annum vs 6 per cent during normal years.  Surprisingly though, the effect on food inflation is not so clear. While it has been higher during El Nino years, the adverse impact during all rainfall-deficit years is not as prominent.  Overall, a fall of 1.2 per cent Y-o-Y in area sown under kharif crops is not reliable evidence to suggest no adverse impact of El Nino. With a similar fall in area sown, we have seen a sharp fall in yield, and thus production, during bad monsoon years earlier.    What about improved irrigation levels or the declining share of agriculture in GVA and, consequently, in GDP? Irrigated area has increased across various crops; however, it remains low. About 70 per cent of the area under rice cultivation was irrigated in 2023-24, compared with 60 per cent a decade earlier and about 55 per cent in the mid-2000s. Similarly, about 35 per cent of the area under pulses was irrigated, compared with 20 per cent a decade earlier. This is one of the reasons why we don’t expect a decline in real agricultural GVA in FY27, despite a super El Nino and a large rainfall deficit.  Moreover, while the share of crops in the total agricultural GVA was falling from 65 per cent in FY12/FY13 to 54 per cent in FY24 (under the 2011-12 base), it was revised upwards to 62 per cent in FY23 under the new 2022-23 base and has remained unchanged through FY25.  To conclude, we firmly believe that the adverse impact of El Nino and a large rainfall deficit will be visible in 2HFY27. That’s why, we find it really difficult to believe that real GVA/GDP growth could stay at 6.8-6.9 per cent in 2HFY27, as is suggested by the Reserve Bank of India projections and the market consensus. Including an unfavourable base effect, weak fiscal spending growth (since we assume that the government will meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.5 per cent of GDP), and the adverse impact of higher inflation on consumption, we believe that GVA/GDP growth could weaken substantially to below 6 per cent. This will also make it difficult for the RBI to raise rates after December, making this rate-hike episode a shallow one. 
 The writer is India economist at CLSA India Private Ltd and the author of The Eight Per Cent Solution     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Navigating Europe's regulatory maze
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Navigating Europe's regulatory mazeNavigating Europe's regulatory maze

Market access to the EU is shifting from tariff barriers to regulatory requirements

premium

Tighter EU trade and sustainability rules are raising compliance costs and reshaping market access for Indian exporters

Sangeeth SelvarajuPrachi Priya5 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTThe European Union’s recent decision to tighten steel import restrictions highlights the emerging shifts in the global trade landscape. From July 2026, the EU replaced its existing steel safeguard regime with a new framework that reduced duty-free tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) by roughly 47 per cent and increased the out-of-quota duty from 25 per cent to 50 per cent. The new framework also expanded the range of steel product categories covered and introduced stricter traceability requirements, including “melt-and-pour” reporting, which requires importers to identify where the steel was originally melted and cast. By June 30, 2027, the European Commission will assess whether the framework’s scope should be extended to downstream goods manufactured from steel or containing significant amounts of it.   The steel TRQ decision is only one part of a broader European regulatory “spaghetti bowl” that includes the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), Digital Product Passports, the EU Deforestation Regulation, REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals), the Battery Regulation and new waste shipment rules.  While each measure may be justified on environmental, consumer protection or industrial policy grounds, together they are reshaping market access by linking trade more closely to carbon performance, product sustainability, supply-chain due diligence and traceability. For exporters, the challenge is no longer just tariffs, but navigating an increasingly dense web of regulatory compliance.   These measures affect exporters in different ways. Some act as border measures, directly impacting exporter entry into the EU market (such as CBAM, steel tariff-rate quotas ). Others are product-specific requirements that must be met before goods can be sold in Europe (such as ESPR, Digital Product Passports, REACH and the Battery Regulation). A third category operates through supply-chain regulations, such as the CSRD and CSDDD, which require European companies to obtain detailed information on sustainability, emissions and traceability from suppliers worldwide.  Alongside these measures is the EU’s extensive framework of technical regulations and standards, including REACH, CE marking for European conformity, packaging and product safety requirements. Though less visible than CBAM, they can act as barriers through testing, certification, documentation and ongoing compliance obligations.  Perhaps the least discussed but most revealing example is the revised EU Waste Shipment Regulation. The EU has tightened controls on exports of waste, particularly to non- Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries, unless those countries can demonstrate environmentally sound waste management systems. The regulation affects scrap traders, recyclers and processors. While framed as an environmental measure, it can effectively retain critical low-carbon raw materials within Europe. For aluminium and steel producers, this can reduce scrap availability, increase costs for producers elsewhere, and complicate decarbonisation efforts. Europe is, therefore, not only regulating products entering its market but also shaping access to the materials needed to produce them.  Viewed together, these measures represent a fundamental shift in the nature of trade barriers. A steel or aluminium exporter may need to provide emissions data under CBAM, sustainability disclosures for CSRD or CSDDD through value chain, product-level information under ESPR, compliance declarations under REACH, and traceability records under sector-specific regulations. This is before considering TRQs, anti-dumping measures, conformity assessments and other technical standards. Even if free-trade agreements or FTAs reduce tariffs to zero, exporters will still need to navigate this increasingly complex regulatory architecture. Market access, therefore, is shifting from tariff barriers to regulatory requirements.  For India, the priority is to institutionalise engagement with the EU, rather than respond to regulations one by one. First, the government should establish an inter-ministerial coordination mechanism to monitor emerging EU regulations and assess their implications for India. Given that these measures increasingly cut across sectors and ministries, including commerce, power, new & renewable energy, steel, mines, heavy industries and environment, a coordinated platform involving relevant ministries and industry bodies would help develop informed positions and ensure timely engagement with the EU during the EU consultation process.  Second,  India should use the India–EU FTA to establish a formal regulatory cooperation mechanism, such as an India-EU Regulatory Help Desk. Such a platform (with representation from industry bodies) could provide early notification of proposed regulations with significant trade implications, facilitate dialogue on standards, and MRV (measurement, reporting and verification) procedures, promote the recognition of equivalent measures where appropriate, and advocate reasonable transition periods for compliance.  Third, India should develop a mechanism to calculate the actual compliance and trade costs of EU regulations by collecting data on certification costs, compliance time, rejected or delayed consignments, and their impact on industries, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This evidence-based approach would strengthen India’s engagement with the EU and its participation in committees of the World Trade Organization.  Fourth, India should build issue-specific coalitions with other developing countries to engage with the EU on regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens. The objective should not be to oppose sustainability goals, but to ensure that their implementation takes into account differences in levels of economic development, technical expertise and institutional capacity across countries. This should include advocating phased implementation where justified, alongside technical cooperation, knowledge sharing and capacity-building to help industries adapt to the new requirements.  And finally, industry will have to take greater ownership of domestic preparedness. Investments today in supply chain due diligence, MRV traceability, emissions measurement, product-level data systems, and certifications standards will only help make Indian industry future-ready. Industry associations can further support micro, small and medium-sized enterprises by developing shared compliance platforms and providing technical assistance to help them meet evolving regulatory requirements.
The writers are, respectively, a policy fellow at the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics and a Mumbai-based economist     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Prospects of reviving asset sale
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Prospects of reviving asset saleProspects of reviving asset sale

The disinvestment journey of the past decade has not been impressive. How it pans out now depends on some key factors

premium

Illustration: Binay SInha

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 5:32 PM ISTThe Narendra Modi government appears to be on a disinvestment drive. This is happening after a slow and halting implementation of its policy on strategic sale of public-sector undertakings (PSUs) it had announced in 2021.   Last week, the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to sell over 30 per cent of the government’s total equity in IDBI Bank at a price that should yield the central exchequer a disinvestment receipt of over ₹26,500 crore in the current year. With more than five months to go before the current year ends, the government will have collected more than its annual target of ₹80,000 crore from such asset sales during 2026-27. Equally important, the IDBI Bank deal means that the Modi government has now given a push to privatisation after a pause.  It is also important to note that the IDBI Bank privatisation doesn’t appear to be a flash in the pan. According to the finance ministry, the government plans to list three more PSUs on the stock exchange — India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd (IIFCL), Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd (MCL) and South Eastern Coalfields Ltd (SECL). Listing MCL and SECL may not result in any disinvestment receipts for the government, as they are wholly-owned subsidiaries of Coal India Ltd (CIL), which alone will benefit from such share sale proceeds. But the listing decision on IIFCL, wholly owned by the government, will mean more disinvestment receipt if it is listed before March 2027 as planned. Indeed, preparations for an initial public offer of IIFCL shares have already begun.   To be sure, the government’s track record on privatisation so far has been unimpressive. After formulating a policy on strategic disinvestment in 2021, wherein the government decided to exit all PSUs barring a few strategic ones, only Air India, Ferro Scrap Nigam, Neelachal Ispat Nigam and Indian Medicines Pharmaceuticals Corporation have been privatised. Air India was a high-profile company, but owing to its huge, accumulated debt, the net proceeds for the government from its privatisation in January 2022 were only ₹2,700 crore.   Not that the sale of the other three companies saw higher realisation. The privatisation of Ferro Scrap and Neelachal Ispat yielded zero receipts. The sale proceed from Indian Medicines Pharmaceuticals Corporation was ₹118.73 crore. That meant four cases of privatisation got the government only ₹2,818.73 crore. Critics of the government’s privatisation policy have not yet latched on to this number, but when they do, reservations about the policy on strategic sale of PSUs will only get more serious.   In the last twelve and a half years of the Modi government, total disinvestment receipts are estimated at ₹4.37 trillion, of which privatisation proceeds account for a tiny proportion of just 0.64 per cent, with the remaining amount being collected through the sale of minority shares. In the last one and a half years, asset monetisation (or the sale of land and buildings owned by government-owned PSUs) has picked up, with a total amount estimated at ₹34,787 crore. Even after including asset monetisation, total disinvestment proceeds in the Modi regime so far have been less than PSU dividend receipts of ₹5.32 trillion during this period.   This is perhaps one of the reasons for the government slowing down its disinvestment programme from 2021-22, ironically the same year when the government announced its policy on strategic sale of PSUs. It was argued by senior finance ministry functionaries then that value maximisation  was as important an objective in managing PSU assets as achieving disinvestment targets. This reflected a shift in strategy that was no longer overly dependent on strategic disinvestment and required a broader and more holistic approach decoupled from fiscal management.   Not surprisingly, the change in approach was visible in slowing disinvestment receipts, rising dividends from PSUs, and a sharp increase in the government’s equity contribution and loans released to PSUs in subsequent years. Between 2021-22 and 2025-26, disinvestment receipts were estimated at just about 21 per cent of the total such proceeds during the twelve and a half years of the Modi government. In the same period, however, PSU dividends rose to ₹3.35 trillion, accounting for 63 per cent of total received by the government. And the government’s equity and loans to PSUs in this period rose to ₹21.45 trillion, over 57 per cent of what was allocated from 2014-15 to 2026-27. It was during the same period that the government’s Budget documents stopped referring to disinvestment in its capital receipts calculations. In what seemed to be part of its plan to de-emphasise disinvestment, all receipts from asset sales were classified as non-debt capital receipts.    Now that the government’s approach to disinvestment is changing, it will be important to keep track of a few parameters of the government’s receipts and expenditure allocations. One, it will be helpful if disinvestment receipts and asset monetisation receipts are clearly identified in the receipts budget, so that these numbers can be easily identified and subjected to analysis and dissemination.  Two, tracking disinvestment numbers will be important. But equally important will be the need to measure the pace at which the government is investing in PSUs through equity contribution and loans. In the early years of the Modi government, the amount allocated for equity and loans to PSUs was a little more than a third of the government’s total capital expenditure budget. In the last few years, this share has been close to 50 per cent. This trend should be reversed without any decline in the government’s overall capex target.   Three, it will be necessary to keep a close watch on the ratio between the government’s total receipts from PSUs (through disinvestment and dividend income) and the amount it spends on them through equity and loans. In the last five years, the amount of government receipts from PSUs as a share of total spending on PSUs has steadily fallen from around 30 per cent in 2021-22 to 15 per cent in 2024-25, before recovering a bit to about 26 per cent in 2025-26. This ratio should get better over time as the government’s disinvestment receipts increase and the need for fresh equity infusion declines.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India has expanded higher education. Now it must build on it
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India has expanded higher education. Now it must build on itIndia has expanded higher education. Now it must build on it

India must address faculty vacancies, skills gaps and examination flaws to make educational opportunity more equitable

premium

Students at a higher education institution in India, representing the need for equitable access and examination reforms.

Soumya Kanti GhoshShashidharan Sharma7 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTIndia’s higher education map has changed significantly in the last 12 years. Higher education infrastructure is proliferating. As of financial year 2023-24 (FY24), India had 1,289 universities, 48,246 colleges and 15,221 stand-alone institutes, an average growth of 47 per cent over FY14. Reported teachers increased from about 1.37 million to 1.73 million, while women’s share of the teaching workforce rose from 39 per cent to 45 per cent. The share of scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and other backward classes (SC, ST, OBC) jumped to 45 per cent from 32 per cent a decade back. Total enrolment reached 45 million in 2023–24, against 34.2 million in 2014–15, of which PhD enrolment stood at 344,000, with women accounting for almost 50 per cent. SC, ST and OBC enrolment was at 62 per cent in FY24 and girls outnumbered boys in science stream.   The Centre also expanded the premier network. The total number of Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) and National Institutes of Technology (NITs) have expanded from 59 in FY14 to 76 in FY26, with addition of seven IITs, nine IIMs and one NIT. The combined students at IITs and NITs stood at around 244,000 in FY24, against around 162,000 in FY18 — a 27 per cent growth. Using the same institutions at both endpoints during both academic years FY18 and FY24, core-programme enrolment rose by about 58 per cent across the same 17 IITs, 39 per cent across the same 14 IIMs and 30 per cent across the same 22 NITs. This is growth inside the institutions themselves, not arithmetic created by adding new names.    The composition of the classroom has changed too. Women’s share of core undergraduate enrolment at IITs rose from 8 per cent to 20 per cent during FY18 and FY24. At IIMs, women’s share of core postgraduate enrolment rose from 26.3 per cent to 37.7 per cent; at NITs, their share of core undergraduate enrolment increased from 18.4 per cent to 21.8 per cent.   Employers did not mark down the larger graduating classes. More students were placed at higher reported median pay (105 per cent growth in FY24 over FY16). The market still rewards technical and managerial capability when it trusts the institution certifying it. IITs, IIMs and NITs are therefore a benchmark, not a description of the college most young Indians attend. Thus, India has expanded higher education to the masses much faster than what one could perceive in the last decade. The time has now come to build on it further.  Firstly, a recent parliamentary committee report recorded vacancy rates of 34 per cent across all national universities, with the highest vacancy at the professor level at 54 per cent. We need to red­uce these vacant positions.   Secondly, actual Union expenditure by the department of higher education almost doubled between FY15 and FY25. Yet its share of total Union expenditure fell from 1.6 per cent in FY18 to 1 per cent in FY25. Higher-education institutions accounted for 12.6 per cent of India’s research and development (R&D) expenditure in FY24, while the country’s total research effort was only 0.84 per cent of gross dome­stic product. We need to target this increase to 1.5 per cent.  Thirdly, the 2025 Periodic Labour Force Survey found that only 31 per cent of people aged 15-29 had received formal vocational or technical training. It is a pity that while hospitals, factories, data centres and modern cities run on technicians, machinists, electricians, operators, care workers and logistics specialists, our social imagination still ranks the office above the workshop. Germany and Switzerland place apprentices inside recognised occupational ladders, while Singapore connects work-study programmes to continuing education. India should apply the same principle.  Fourthly, across private and public universities, affordability and outcomes differ sharply and there needs to be a convergence.  Fifthly, changes must be made for the National Testing Agency (NTA). The NTA was created in 2018 as a registered society but not by a dedicated statute. According to the Ministry of Education’s written reply to the Rajya Sabha on July 31, 2024, a total of 194 personnel were reported at NTA, excluding the director-general. These included 171 contractual or outsourced workers.  Meanwhile, the government, following the controversies of 2024 and the Radhakrishnan Committee report, has added senior posts and introduced district coordination, centre audits, command-centre monitoring and biometric exception procedures. The Public Examinations Act has now strengthened deterrence against organised unfair means. These steps matter.   China’s Gaokao examination system is useful not because it is flawless, but because it treats redundancy as part of fairness. In 2026, 12.9 million candidates registered across 7,981 centres and roughly 348,000 examination rooms, backed by about 21,000 reserve rooms; more than 14,000 candidates with disabilities received accommodation. Provincial administrations coordinate secure custody, monitored transport and storage, emergency planning, policing, traffic and health support. The practical lesson is to plan for the exam day that goes wrong. When floods blocked access in Anhui province in 2020, two papers were postponed, reserve papers prepared and local transport mobilised. However, we must also appreciate that by July 2024, NTA did conduct more than 240 examinations, serving more than 54 million candidates. In addition, in 2025, the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) conduct­ed 10 exams for appointme­nts to clerical posts involving 18.5 million applications.  We propose four changes that would make the examination system feel less like a black box and more like a public institution emulating the global experience, particularly from China’s Gaokao.   NTA needs firmer foundations. A dedicated law making it accountable to parliament and independent scrutiny, including CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General of India) audit. NTA should build a permanent team of specialists, technologists and security professionals backed by a board that is clearly responsible when systems or vendors fail.  Creation of a candidate charter to promise time-bound decisions on disputed answers, translation mistakes, incorrect scores, disrupted examinations and re-tests. An appeal decided after admissions have closed is no remedy at all.  NTA should publish an annual account of disruptions, leaks, re-tests, appeals, vendor failures and corrective action.   NTA should immediately move over to computer- based tests along the lines of the joint entrance examination (JEE), with multiple dates spread over morning and afternoon sessions and the best score counted over two attempts, say in January and April. The entire application process may be mimick­ed along the lines of JEE or even the SSC exam pattern.  Finally, for millions of young Indians, an examination is a bridge between circumstance and aspiration. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution protects a life of dignity, Article 14 forbids arbitrary State action, and Article 21A establishes that education is a constitutional commitment, not an act of charity. We propose that Article 21 be amended to support a right to free and fair educational opportunity. Free should mean freedom from fraud, discrimination and unreasonable barriers.   Fair must mean transparent rules, secure examinations, accurate evaluation and an effective remedy when the system fails. A student cannot demand a rank, but she is entitled to demand an honest race. Let us make a beginning.   Ghosh is member, 16th Finance Commission and PMEAC, and group chief economic advisor, State Bank of India. Sharma is economist, State Bank of India. Views are personal.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's WTO moment is now
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's WTO moment is nowIndia's WTO moment is now

Along with other middle powers, India must step up to revive the WTO and help reshape its rules in the interests of the Global South

premium

India has an opportunity to lead efforts to reform the World Trade Organization, strengthen multilateral trade rules and safeguard the interests of developing economies. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Dammu Ravi6 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe World Trade Organization’s Global Trade Outlook, released in October 2026, presents a surprising headline: World merchandise trade volume grew by 4.2 per cent in 2025, up from 2.8 per cent in 2024. This surge has come despite geopolitical headwinds — the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, unilateral tariffs, and chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. As WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala notes, nearly 72 per cent of world trade is still conducted on a most-favoured-nation (MFN) basis, reflecting enduring faith in the rules-based multilateral architecture. This optimism, however, masks a deeper reality that confronts a large number of developing countries. The case, therefore, is not just for a revival of the WTO but also for its urgent reform.

 Revisiting foundational principles

When the WTO was founded in 1995, the world was neatly divided into developed and developing countries. The underlying philosophy was to help developing countries integrate into the world economy with flexibilities built in through Special and Differential Treatment (S&DT) and consensus-based decision-making. These were foundational principles designed to prevent majoritarian manipulation and coercion through coalitions. Thirty years on, these principles warrant a closer look.  

 The rise of emerging economies

 The S&DT concessions granted in 1995 were well-intentioned. What was not envisaged was how economic status would evolve — some countries graduating, others falling behind. The last two decades have seen the resurgence of emerging market economies (EMEs). About 30 large EMEs today are the driving force of the global economy, accounting for an estimated $6.7 trillion of the $26.26 trillion in world merchandise exports in 2025. If services are included, the value rises to $8.75 trillion.  

S&DT, consensus and MFN: The dilemma

 Developed countries and EMEs together number about 60 of the WTO’s 166 members. The remaining members are low-income developing countries and least developed countries (LDCs), whose combined share of global trade is no more than 10 per cent. Making a separate category for EMEs is politically sensitive — it risks fragmenting the solidarity of the Global South and weakening its collective leverage, a fragmentation developed countries have long sought to highlight. Aspirational countries need greater flexibilities to meet development objectives while the poorest seek even greater concessions and market access, including from EMEs.  The way forward may be for EMEs to voluntarily forgo some S&DT flexibilities, each according to its level of comfort. If India shows the way, others may follow. India can credibly lead this transition even in the most sensitive areas. In agriculture, it can shift support from Amber to Green Box through decoupled direct benefit transfers in place of price-linked minimum support price-based procurement. Such decoupled income support — not linked to production, prices or factors of production — qualifies as Green Box under Annex 2 of the Agreement on Agriculture and is exempt from reduction commitments. This would ensure benefits reach poor and marginal farmers without leakages.  Accumulation of foodgrains far beyond the requirements of the public distribution system is a huge drain on the exchequer, besides encouraging the overuse of agro-chemicals and depletion of precious groundwater. The same principle can guide India’s approach to the fisheries subsidies negotiations — replacing capacity-enhancing fuel and vessel subsidies with targeted, sustainability-linked income support for fisher families.  Such transitions would give India the moral authority to argue for changes in the rulebook in the larger interest of developing countries. The ability to subsume a national position within the lowest common denominator of a larger rulebook is a skill India needs to nurture if it is to assume a leadership role at the WTO.  Similarly, the principle of Consensus, however well-intentioned, was inherently flawed. It presumed convergence among members despite vastly divergent economic strengths. In practice, even a small country can hold negotiations hostage and block outcomes, including Ministerial Declarations — as seen at the Eleventh Ministerial Conference (MC11) in Buenos Aires in 2017 and at MC14 in Cameroon in March 2026, where hosts had to settle for a Chair’s Summary. Some modification is necessary to prevent such logjams. The model used for the Trade Facilitation Agreement in 2014 is worth exploring: Members agree in principle by consensus, but implementation follows differentiated timelines based on each member’s preparedness, while developed countries take on obligations from day one.  Another pillar — MFN, which ensures non-discriminatory market access — has been undermined by unilateral tariffs. As Ms Okonjo-Iweala has repeatedly stressed, while over 70 per cent of trade still flows under MFN, the erosion is real. The long-term implication is clear: Countries will seek to offset MFN distortions through bilateral and plurilateral free-trade agreements (FTAs), a trend that does not augur well for developing countries outside the FTA architecture. While many will continue to abide by MFN trade, the new frontier is non-tariff barriers — regulatory friction, standards, conformity assessment, and logistics facilitation. Active Indian engagement here can help steer balanced outcomes in the interest of the Global South.  

Plurilaterals are integral to trade

 The plurilateral initiatives first proposed at MC11 — investment facilitation, MSMEs or micro, small and medium enterprises, ecommerce and gender — have become contentious. India’s position that these are non-trade issues is increasingly untenable. In a highly interdependent global economy, these issues are integral to trade. India has already taken commitments on them in bilateral agreements, yet hesitates to participate in multilateral rule-making at the WTO.  In fact, the New Delhi Brics Declaration of September 2026 has itself recognised the importance of identifying “appropriate pathways for plurilateral initiatives into the WTO legal framework”. Staying out is not an option — rules made outside by a critical mass inevitably impact outsiders. India’s participation can ensure balance and defend the interests of the Global South.  

The crown jewel: Dispute settlement

 The Dispute Settlement Mechanism, the crown jewel of the WTO, has been crippled since 2017 when the US blocked appointments to the Appellate Body. It was a major blow to a system seen as ensuring fairness and equity. The European Union’s alternative model — with mediation, non-appeal settlements and enforcement — could be a starting point. It calls for creative thinking. India’s long experience in trade disputes, both at the WTO and bilaterally, can add immense value in crafting an acceptable model for all.  

India can lead

 It is time for India to actively participate in reviving the WTO. If middle powers, including the EU, come forward, the chances of revival will brighten. Canada’s idea of middle powers leading the WTO's revival is worth serious deliberation — and India is well-placed to lead it.

entry.title: Rupee volatility is a signal
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Rupee volatility is a signalRupee volatility is a signal

The world is changing structurally, and India needs to adjust

premium

The rupee's volatility and declining foreign exchange reserves highlight growing pressure on India's external sector amid foreign capital outflows, rising crude prices and higher global bond yields. | Representative Picture

Rajesh Kumar5 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 10:02 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is fighting a difficult battle to keep the rupee stable. It is intervening in the foreign exchange market and has imposed several restrictions on currency derivatives to curb speculation. It also raised foreign currency through special swap schemes, including the one for non-resident Indians. The response to the scheme was encouraging, with banks mobilising about $133 billion through Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR (B), deposits. This helped take India’s foreign exchange reserves to a record high of $785.71 billion in the week ended September 4.  Some saw the mobilisation as an effort to build buffers in an uncertain economic environment, though the RBI had reserves worth over $680 billion when it announced the step. As things stand, the reserves have declined by about $60 billion from the record highs. Part of the decline can possibly be explained by revaluation to reflect the actual value of the assets the central bank holds. But it also suggests that the RBI is intervening aggressively in the market.  The RBI’s stated policy is that it intervenes in the market only to address excess volatility and does not target any level. However, in the present circumstances, it does appear to be chasing other objectives as well, perhaps to prevent the rupee from breaching a certain level. The rupee at 100 against the dollar, for instance, would make headlines and become a political issue. However, for economic policy managers, this number should not matter much. In fact, what should matter is that at the current rate of decline in reserves, the FCNR (B) buffer will quickly disappear. The FCNR (B) mobilisation showed that India can quickly raise significant amounts of foreign funds in a short period of time, but such an option cannot be used again in the near term.  At the fundamental level, what is needed is a dispassionate assessment of the situation and appropriate adjustments in domestic policies. One explanation for currency market volatility is the West Asia crisis and its sustained impact on crude-oil prices. This is a reasonable concern. With no clear resolution road map in sight, higher energy prices will continue to influence sentiment in the currency market. However, it is worth highlighting that India faced a balance of payments (BoP) deficit in the previous two financial  years as well.  India usually runs a current account deficit (CAD), which is financed by global capital flows. There is nothing inherently wrong with running a reasonable CAD. Foreign capital supplements domestic savings and is an important part of India’s broader macroeconomic management structure. Even the fiscal responsibility and budget management (FRBM) framework took into account the availability of foreign savings.  However, what has happened in recent periods is that India has not been able to attract and retain enough foreign capital. Foreign portfolio investors, for instance, have sold Indian financial assets worth over $26 billion so far in 2026. Thus, the issue is not limited to the CAD. In fact, professional forecasters’ projection— published in the latest Monetary Policy Report of the RBI— for CAD in the current financial year is 1.2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), which cannot be termed as alarming in normal circumstances. The bigger problem is the capital account.  So why is India not attracting enough capital? There are at least two explanations. First, increasing investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and related areas is absorbing capital from around the world. Since India is not in the AI play in any significant manner, it is unable to draw foreign flows. The AI boom is also one of the reasons Indian stock markets have underperformed and are witnessing outflows of foreign funds. Reports suggest that AI investment may be slowing. It is also being argued globally that investment in AI and the valuations of related companies are showing signs of a bubble. There is a view that once this bubble bursts, funds will get redirected to markets like India.  This sounds more like hope, and Indian policy managers must not buy such arguments. On the contrary, a burst or a significant correction in valuations could lead to considerable global financial instability, if not a crisis. Trillions of dollars are being invested in AI infrastructure, and an increasingly large proportion of this investment is being financed through debt and other complex instruments that are difficult to track. Experience shows that a substantial increase in global financial uncertainty results in capital shifting to safe assets, not emerging markets. Thus, a burst could end up putting more pressure on capital flows, at least for a while, and India must be prepared for it.  Second, higher bond yields in the developed world are affecting flows. If a global fund manager can earn over 5 per cent annually by simply holding US government bonds, considered to be the safest in the world, why take the risk of investing in emerging markets? However, this should have been anticipated. Public debt has increased substantially in the developed world, including the US, where it is moving up structurally. According to the International Monetary Fund, government borrowing requirement in advanced economies this year will be worth about 5.2 per cent of GDP, the highest since Covid. Public debt stock in the US is expected to increase to over 142 per cent of GDP by 2031 — up from about 109 per cent in 2019.  Thus, the world is changing structurally, and India needs to adjust. The playbook on both the current and capital accounts is well known. Leaving the adjustment reluctantly to the currency market alone could become painful beyond a point.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Not in default, but already affected
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Not in default, but already affectedNot in default, but already affected

Evaluating the IBC primarily through resolution outcomes provides only a partial picture of its effects

premium

In its early years, the IBC was widely credited with improving India’s previously dysfunctional corporate insolvency resolution framework

Aaraadhya SrivastavaPratibha KumariJithin P5 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTThe Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), a landmark reform introduced during the first term of the Modi government, marked its 10th anniversary in May 2026. Commentaries assessing the IBC’s performance have critiqued it on three grounds: (1) delays in the resolution process, (2) the relatively large share of concluded cases ending in liquidation rather than restructuring, and (3) the large haircuts suffered by creditors.  These are valid concerns regarding the functioning of the IBC once a firm enters insolvency proceedings. However, these very features determine what lenders expect to recover upon default and, consequently, shape the terms on which they extend credit before any default occurs. Thus, evaluating the IBC primarily through resolution outcomes provides only a partial picture of its effects. We, therefore, look beyond the insolvency process to examine how the reform affected firms that never entered insolvency proceedings.  In its early years, the IBC was widely credited with improving India’s previously dysfunctional corporate insolvency resolution framework. Before the IBC, creditors recovered barely a quarter of the value of distressed assets, while resolution often took more than four years, according to the World Bank’s Doing Business 2015 report. By 2020, recovery rates under the IBC had risen to over 45 per cent, while average resolution time had fallen to around 413 days, a remarkable turnaround from the multi-year delays of the past. This early period provides a useful setting for understanding the effects of improvements in the insolvency resolution process, before subsequent challenges weakened these gains.  Quicker resolution reduced the deadweight costs associated with lengthy bankruptcy proceedings, while higher recovery rates strengthened lenders’ confidence in the enforceability of their claims. With lower expected losses in the event of default, lenders had greater incentives to expand the supply of credit and lend at a lower cost than before. Research supports this argument.In a 2021 paper published in the Journal of Corporate Finance, Bose, Filomeni, and Mallick document that the IBC expanded the availability of low-cost credit to distressed firms.  Distressed firms, in turn, had an incentive to use their additional borrowing capacity to finance risky projects. Why? Because if such projects succeeded, the resulting improvement in cash flows could allow firms to avoid default. Consistent with this possibility, Singh, Chauhan, and Jadiyappa (2022), in a paper published in Finance Research Letters, document that the IBC induced distressed firms to take on more risk than non-distressed firms, with the increase in risk-taking accompanied by improved operating performance. These results suggest that a bankruptcy law that rapidly resolves insolvency, as the IBC did during its initial years, can both enable creditors to recover a larger fraction of their dues more quickly and improve the prospects of distressed firms.  These findings should not, however, imply that the IBC mattered only for distressed firms. The reform could also have affected the financing and investment decisions of relatively healthy firms. How? By improving expected recovery for lenders and making the insolvency process more time-bound, the IBC may have increased the amount of credit that lenders were willing to extend against a given pool of collateral. Firms with a greater stock of collateralisable assets could then have accessed additional debt to finance value-enhancing activities such as capital-goods imports, which can serve as a source of technological upgrading. We tested this hypothesis and found that, following the introduction of the IBC, import-dependent firms with more pledgeable assets borrowed more and used the additional funds to increase their capital-goods imports by about 31 per cent relative to otherwise comparable firms.  Put together, these findings suggest that the IBC has consequences even for firms that never enter insolvency. Its influence, however, depends on lenders perceiving it as a credible mechanism for timely recovery. Recent evidence of prolonged insolvency proceedings raises concerns in this regard. According to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India newsletter for the April-June 2026 quarter, the average time taken to complete a restructuring process was 1,026 days, while the average liquidation process took 1,378 days. Such delays may undermine lenders’ confidence in the framework, with implications for the supply and cost of credit. Weaker confidence could, in turn, affect firms’ access to external finance, constrain investment by viable firms, and increase the likelihood of default among financially weaker firms.  The IBC should, therefore, be judged not only by what happens when firms default, but also by how the prospect of default shapes the behaviour of firms and lenders before it occurs. Its greatest contribution may lie not in resolving insolvency after the fact, but in changing behaviour before it does. For that to happen, however, the promise of timely resolution must remain credible.
The writers are, respectively,  assistant professor at the Indian Institute of Management, Ranchi;assistant professor at TAPMI, Bengaluru; and assistant professor at the Indian Institute of Management, Raipur. entry.title: Confronting economic trade-offs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Confronting economic trade-offsConfronting economic trade-offs

Market-driven prices and tax reforms can support monetary policy and attract foreign capital

premium

Rising bond yields, rupee depreciation and uncertain foreign capital flows have renewed the debate over monetary policy, market-driven interest rates and tax reforms in India. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ananth Narayan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 12:04 AM ISTIn a difficult global environment, interest rates have risen, the rupee has weakened, and net foreign-capital flows remain uncertain. It is worth looking at the takeaways from the recent past to consider the road ahead.  What happened? With consumer inflation averaging just 2 per cent in 2025, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) cut the policy repo rate by 125 basis points (bps) to 5.25 per cent. In financial year (FY) 2025-26, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also bought government bonds worth 2.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) to support growth and replenish liquidity drained by foreign exchange outflows. These record RBI bond purchases were 70 per cent higher than those in 2020-21, during the Covid pandemic, and were 85 per cent of the Centre’s net borrowing in FY26.  Indian bond yields consequently fell. The difference between India and US 10-year bond yields declined to multi-decade lows of below 2 percentage points. Given that the difference between inflation in India and the US also narrowed, this may seem reasonable. However, rates should be determined by demand and supply from willing borrowers and lenders. In India, the lender pushing down interest rates was the RBI, not willing savers. For discretionary savers, post-tax returns on fixed-income remained unattractive.  Repressing interest rates so forcefully has consequences. Discretionary savings shifted away from fixed-income investments to equities, contributing to pockets of overvaluation there. Net foreign-inflows struggled, partly due to these high equity valuations. Outward direct investments also rose. Narrower rate differentials compressed dollar-rupee forward premia, making hedging and speculation against the rupee cheaper.  Across FY25 and FY26, the RBI net sold $192 billion in currency markets, much of it to feed hedging and speculative dollar demand. As dollar outflows drained rupee liquidity, markets signalled the need for higher interest rates. Instead, the RBI’s bond purchases and other actions poured durable liquidity into a leaky bucket. Short-term instruments could have replenished liquidity without depressing long-term yields.  The rupee fell from 85 per dollar in January 2025 to 92.5 by mid-February 2026, before the Iran conflict took it towards 97. We sought low rates, currency stability, and capital inflows. Yet despite many large market interventions, subsidised foreign exchange (FX) swaps, and restrictions on currency trading, pressures persist.  Lessons for stakeholders:  Armchair advice, present company included, is easy to dispense. With that acknowledged, three lessons stand out.  First, as the last few years have demonstrated, the impossible trinity matters. Monetary independence, capital mobility and exchange-rate stability involve inevitable trade-offs. The 2014 Urjit Patel Committee recognised this, prioritising inflation control at the time while envisaging greater flexibility once inflation expectations were anchored. Yet the RBI’s August 2025 monetary framework review did not even mention this trilemma.  Second, clear communication about policy choices and trade-offs is essential for market confidence. Pursuing multiple, conflicting objectives simultaneously while avoiding trade-offs risks undermining credibility. We could then end up with the worst of all worlds.  Third, large interventions in interconnected markets risk unintended consequences. Consistency also requires reframing the debate from “let the rupee find its own level” to “let both the rupee and rupee interest rates find their own levels”.  The way forward: Allow market-determined rates. Rather than repressing interest rates with interventions and schemes, we should largely let discretionary savings fund borrowings. Free debt markets should also allow for freer and more stable currency markets.  To be fair, in FY27, the RBI has net sold ₹1.25 trillion of government bonds to absorb liquidity created by its FX swap scheme. The MPC raised the repo rate by 25 bps this month. Yet the current India-US 10-year bond yield spread is at 230 bps, well below its historical median of around 400 bps. It is unclear if this will attract savings into Indian debt.  For credibility, the MPC and RBI must demonstrate the same willingness to tighten monetary conditions as they showed in easing them. Moving banking liquidity towards neutral would give market forces greater scope to determine bond yields.  What about growth?  Higher interest rates can impact growth. However, a lower tax burden on fixed-income can allow for lower headline rates. Interest and some fixed-income capital gains are taxed at marginal income-tax rates, leaving savers with unattractive post-tax returns.  We could tax interest income, including from fixed deposits, at the lower of, say, 20 per cent or the applicable slab rate. Capital gains on debt funds could be taxed on a par with equities.  This would also let risk-return considerations, rather than taxation, drive savings allocation. Tax revenue losses may also be limited, since tax-sensitive savers likely avoid direct fixed-income already.  Remove impediments to foreign portfolio flows:   India is an outlier in taxing capital gains earned by foreign investors on non-controlling portfolio investments in equities and corporate bonds. Most countries allow such gains to be taxed where the investor resides. Indian tax residents investing in overseas securities largely pay capital gains tax only in India.  Residence-based taxation is, therefore, not a discriminatory tax exemption only for foreigners. Their gains remain subject to tax rules in their home countries. Tax treaties do not fully address this irritant. Many foreign investors cannot offset Indian taxes against their home taxes. They may also pay Indian tax on rupee gains even when their dollar returns are poor. Compliance adds further to costs and complexity.  India’s June 2026 tax relief for qualifying foreign investment in government securities offers a useful precedent. Extending such residence-based taxation to corporate bonds and equities would significantly ease foreign investment. An increase in the securities transaction tax for foreign investors, particularly on high-turnover derivatives, could offset the resulting loss in tax revenue. These reforms cannot guarantee foreign inflows in an uncertain world. But they would remove distortions and allow for more palatable policy trade-offs.  Strengthen tax policy consultation:  Capital-market tax reforms deserve comprehensive consultation, akin to the ones that regulators undertake.  This can bring in expertise and clarity and enhance policy credibility. India retains meaningful buffers and macroeconomic strength. Credible policies, backed by clear communication that confronts difficult trade-offs, will help us navigate these uncertain times.

entry.title: RBI's rupee fix: What is it solving?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / RBI's rupee fix: What is it solving?RBI's rupee fix: What is it solving?

As the central bank announces a new set of bold regulatory measure, this question is worth asking

premium

The RBI's latest forex regulations have raised concerns over higher currency hedging costs and their potential impact on investment and the rupee | Representative Picture

Rajeswari Sengupta5 min read Last Updated : Oct 19 2026 | 10:16 PM ISTWhen the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) announced the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR (B), scheme in June 2026 to attract dollar inflows, many saw it as a turning point in the battle to stabilise the rupee. A few of us were sceptical. Now, the RBI has announced a new set of bold regulatory measures. Should we be sceptical again?  Understanding the past is key to ascertaining the future. So, let’s review. The RBI ended the FCNR(B) scheme on August 31, a month earlier than planned, suggesting that the $133 billion that the scheme had attracted was more than sufficient. Yet on October 10, the RBI tightened foreign exchange regulations significantly, including imposing a hefty tax on forward purchases of dollars. Naturally, people are asking: Why were these measures necessary if the FCNR(B) scheme was hailed as a success?  The answer is not clear. The RBI has mentioned the need to preserve financial stability, but surely the Indian financial system is not in any danger. In the absence of a clear official explanation, the public is left to figure out what problem these measures are meant to address, whether they will succeed or whether their benefits will outweigh the costs to the economy. Let’s try to address these questions.  There are two possible explanations for why the rupee has been depreciating for such a long time: Sentiment towards the Indian economy has soured or India’s balance of payments (BoP) is suffering from structural shocks.  Consider the case where the problem is merely one of sentiment. In that case, it may be reasonable to think that strong measures could jolt the market back to its senses.  Reasonable, but wrong. We know this because that strategy has already been tried and it didn’t work. Despite the huge FCNR (B) inflows, the RBI has continued to actively intervene in the foreign exchange markets and, according to some estimates, it has already used up nearly half the dollar inflows mobilised through various concessional swap schemes introduced since June 2026, including the FCNR(B) scheme. Yet the rupee has continued to depreciate. And it now seems that these schemes were not enough, which is why the RBI has resorted to regulatory interventions.  This suggests that the rupee’s decline may not merely be a problem of worsening sentiment; it could be a structural story. In fact, over the last couple of years, India has been hit by a series of macroeconomic shocks, such as falling behind in the development of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models and the West Asia war, which has imposed a huge energy bill on the country. Perhaps the most disappointing has been the realisation that “China+1” did not translate into a shift of global manufacturing to India, as can be seen from the low levels of foreign direct investment.  If these are indeed the underlying factors responsible for the rupee’s persistent decline, then yet another round of palliative measures will, at best, provide short-term relief. It is true that palliatives can at times be useful, as a way to buy time until more fundamental cures are implemented. However, the problem in this case is that the benefits of the recent measures are likely to be small, and will be exceeded by their costs.  First, the sudden imposition of such stringent measures so soon after the “successful” June 2026 schemes, suggests to the market that the RBI is deeply worried about India’s BoP prospects. It signals that the RBI has concluded that conditions are so fragile that conventional interventions in the spot and forward markets are no longer enough to manage currency volatility. It is then natural for foreign investors to worry as well. In other words, rather than restoring confidence, the RBI’s new measures risk reinforcing the very pessimism they are meant to address.  Second, the new measures have already resulted in a big jump in currency hedging costs. According to some reports, the one-year forward premium has risen above 4.5 per cent, its highest level since January 2022. For importers, exporters or investors using forward contracts to buy or sell dollars in the future, a higher forward premium means it becomes more expensive to hedge currency risk. This is particularly costly for Indian manufacturers, many of whom depend heavily on imported inputs. As hedging becomes more expensive, they will now be forced to bear greater currency risk themselves. This uncertainty can further discourage them from investing, the exact opposite of what the economy needs.  In the end, the latest measures announced by the RBI are unlikely to stem the rupee’s decline, but they risk imposing further costs on an economy where underlying growth momentum remains weak. This brings us back to the central question: What prompted the RBI to take such drastic steps? It is important for the central bank to explain the rationale behind its decision and how it expects the benefits to outweigh the costs.

entry.title: Growing cyber risks
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Growing cyber risksGrowing cyber risks

Threats call for stronger systemic safeguards

premium

SBI says its operations and financial performance remain unaffected and is investigating the source and extent of the exposure | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 9:58 PM ISTState Bank of India’s (SBI’s) disclosure that 3,897 customer records containing personal information were identified among about the 375,000  found on the dark web is a reminder that cybersecurity is no longer merely an information-technology (IT) concern. The exposed pieces of information reportedly include mobile numbers, addresses, dates of birth and loan-related details. SBI says its operations and financial performance remain unaffected and is investigating the source and extent of the exposure. But for customers, the concern is different. Such information can make impersonation, phishing and other fraud more credible. The fact that SBI was alerted by the threat-intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) also raises questions about the ability of large institutions to detect breaches themselves.  The risks extend beyond data theft. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data shows that digital-payment frauds account for the largest number of cases of bank fraud. CERT-In has also warned of attacks on non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lenders, fintechs, payment-service providers, and wallets. The threat is becoming harder to contain because artificial intelligence (AI) lowers the cost and time of attacks. Earlier this month, CERT-In issued a critical advisory in which AI agents accessed live systems and confidential records of Indian organisations without authorisation; none of the affected organisations detected the access themselves. Attackers are also using agentic AI tools for financially motivated intrusions. The lesson is that conventional weaknesses, including exposed credentials, poorly secured application programming interface (API), and excessive cloud permissions, become considerably more dangerous when machines can exploit them at speed and scale. The recent eMudhra certificate incident illustrates the wider problem of digital trust. CERT-In has warned that compromised private keys could be used to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. A weakness at any layer, such as banks, fintechs, cloud-service providers, APIs or digital-certification infrastructure, can, therefore, have consequences beyond the organisation directly affected. The regulatory response must consequently go beyond operational resilience. India already has cybersecurity and fraud-risk frameworks under the RBI, while the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, provides for notifying personal-data breaches to affected individuals. Yet the relevant DPDP provisions and rules are subject to staggered commencement, with the principal breach-notification provisions taking effect only 18 months after the November 2025 notification. This leaves a crucial gap in the interim. Informing regulators and reassuring investors are not a substitute for warning customers whose data may have been exposed.  It should be mandated that regulated entities notify affected customers promptly when there is credible evidence of a material personal-data exposure, without waiting for an investigation to establish every detail. Banks and financial firms should also be held to enforceable standards on API security, third-party risk, cloud access, and AI-agent permissions. CERT-In’s guidance on limiting agent access, isolating testing environments, requiring human approval for high-impact actions, and maintaining tamper-resistant logs should become part of operational practice rather than merely advice. India’s digital-financial architecture has expanded rapidly. Its security framework must now evolve at the same pace. The objective should not merely be to ensure that banks continue to function after an attack, but to ensure that customers are protected, informed and able to act when security fails.     Topics : Dark Web sbi cybersecurity Data breach frauds Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: A singular approach
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A singular approachA singular approach

Pollution-control plans must be coordinated across north India

premium

Delhi’s winter pollution-control measures require coordinated action across the National Capital Region and stubble-burning districts to deliver cleaner air (PTI Photo/Shahbaz Khan)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 10:06 PM ISTThe administration of Delhi has been admirably proactive in invoking the first stage of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP I) as soon as the air-quality index (AQI) in the city jumped from 179 to 244 (“poor”) in a day. The first of a four-stage response linked to the AQI levels bans coal and wood burning (including tandoors used in restaurants and open eateries) and the use of diesel-generator sets except in some circumstances. This comes just under a week ahead of Delhi’s winter-pollution action plan, which restricts petrol pumps from dispensing fuel to vehicles without valid pollution-control certificates, bans outside vehicles that do not conform to Bharat-VI emission standards, introduces a 50 per cent work-from-home mandate, doubles parking fees to discourage the use of personal vehicles, and restricts construction. These norms will be in place till the end of February. This early response is a well-meaning attempt to control winter pollution, for which the city has earned a global reputation. However, its efficacy is still to be tested, given the onset of the paddy stubble-burning season, the precipitous drop in wind speed, the monitoring abilities of the Delhi government, and the Diwali fireworks onslaught, which has, inexplicably, not been banned.  But these are only some of the challenges in ensuring that the citizens of Delhi enjoy clean air this coming winter. To work, they need a far wider ambit of enforcement, which is beyond the remit of the Delhi government. Delhi is situated within a wider bustling urban agglomeration termed the National Capital Region, comprising districts in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. Most cities in these states account for the bulk of the urban pollution in India. For Delhi’s winter pollution- control action plan to work, it needs administrations in these areas to introduce reciprocal plans. Beyond the standard restrictions on old vehicles and construction — which have not proved noticeably effective these past winters — there is no evidence of synchronicity in planning. The National Capital Region Planning Board, which comes under the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, could play a useful role in coordinating pollution-control plans.  But this, too, will partially address the problem. The latest data for the AQI ranking shows that Delhi is not one of the 13 Indian cities listed among the top 20 most polluted ones in the world. That distinction goes to Bulandshahr, Pali, Mathura, Muzaffarnagar, Rohtak, Kota, Hapur, Bikaner, Bareilly and Hisar. Only Mumbai, Agartala, and Burhanpur (Madhya Pradesh) fall outside the northern Gangetic belt. Several of these urban polluters lie close to the stubble-burning zones. No northern city is immune to the dense smoke from fires that farmers routinely set to clear their fields ahead of the rabi season. So far, the governments of Haryana and Punjab — ground zero of stubble-burning — have yet to offer viable solutions to a problem that clearly demands intervention from the central government, as it is the result of long-term central agricultural policies. The bottom line, therefore, is that without a coordinated action plan that involves North Indian urban administrations as well as the rural districts, citywise pollution-action plans will prove largely ineffective. For the Union government, getting its act together is no longer a question of politics but of addressing a burgeoning public-health crisis.     Topics : Stubble burning Delhi air pollution winter pollution Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Safety first in road contracts
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Safety first in road contractsSafety first in road contracts

Penalty regime should be backed by rigorous project appraisal

premium

The government's proposed penalties for road construction defects highlight the need for stricter safety inspections and better engineering standards to prevent fatal accidents. | Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ plan to penalise contractors in engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) for deficiencies in road construction leading to fatal accidents marks a significant drive towards enforcing greater accountability and safety in projects. Contractors will be given an opportunity to rectify the error within 15 days of the first accident, with the option for the government to step in to undertake remedial work at the contractor’s cost if the person does not comply within the deadline. If another accident occurs within a year of the first at the same spot or 500 metres from the original location, contractors will be charged ₹25 lakh for each fatality and ₹10 lakh for each grievous injury. Though this punitive framework appears unexceptionable in theory, it amounts to action taken after a tragedy occurs.  The question is whether this move needs to be complemented by a more rigorous project appraisal and inspection regime within the relevant government agencies, to ensure that project design and engineering are optimum in the first place. In a country in which experienced contractors are known to display no mean talent in exploiting contractual weaknesses, zero tolerance should precede a repent-and-pay policy. India has the distinction of having the world’s third-largest road network but also shares with China global leadership in road fatalities. In 2025, India recorded over 183,000 fatalities from over 500,000 accidents, averaging 21 deaths every hour, according to the government data. Poor road design is not the only cause of these. Rash driving and rule breaking too are major contributors, but bad road design does constitute a significant threat. Former Tata Sons chairman Cyrus Mistry’s death in 2022 was partly the result of an engineering flaw on the highway on which he was travelling (though the driver, too, was speeding).  Still, the problem is clearly serious enough for the Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari to flag the issue. Speaking at a road-safety event in August, he identified poorly designed accident-prone stretches or black spots as a major cause of road deaths. He spoke of spending a steep ₹40,000 crore to identify the most vulnerable spots in 100 districts to fix the problem. Though this exercise is good, the question is why it should have been needed. The government uses a mix of models for road construction projects — EPC; the hybrid annuity model, or HAM, part-financed by the government; and the build-operate-transfer or BOT annuity model, in which the government pays the contractor fixed semi-annual amounts.  Typically, payments for road projects are linked to pre-agreed milestones and a portion of the payment is held back for a defect-liability period, which can vary from one to four years. This implies that some level of quality control is baked into contracts. Perhaps the question the government should also be asking is why such a high level of fatality-causing deficiencies happens when a third-party independent engineer or certifier has to sign off on the quality of a road before payment is released. National highways account for over a third of road fatalities. With large highway projects under construction, the need for significantly upgrading the monitoring of engineering and construction quality has become critical. The lives of thousands of Indians depend on it.   Topics : Nitin Gadkari BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Road construction Road safety road accident Road Ministry
