Ambiguity on satellite communication is creating unease

premium

Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite await security clearances to launch commercial satellite broadband services in India, amid delays in regulatory approvals. (AI-generated image)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 9:46 PM ISTThe recent public spat between stakeholders on approvals related to satellite-broadband service in India points to a systemic problem. It started with Elon Musk, chief executive of Texas-headquartered SpaceX and Tesla, hitting out at potential rivals in India, calling them “oligarchs’’ and blaming them for blocking competition. He specifically insinuated that Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL) might have had a role in delaying the security clearance of Starlink, the satellite-internet company operated by SpaceX. RIL rejected the allegations, saying that it welcomed competition and that Jio Satellite Communications too was waiting for security approval. Bharti Enterprises Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal joined the war of words, stating that his company had been in the queue the longest in starting satellite broadband in India. As for the Union government, Minister of Communications Jyotiraditya Scindia retorted by saying that India did not allow monopolies in any sector.  Bharti Enterprises-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, Starlink and Jio Satellite have all been granted the licence to operate satellite-broadband service in India, but they cannot commercially launch operations without security clearance from the government. Eutelsat OneWeb is reported to have got the Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) licence way back in 2021. Jio Satellite got its licence in 2022, while Starlink was able to make the cut in 2025. The fact that the companies armed with the requisite licence are unable to launch commercial operations is a matter of concern and frustration for businesses. Granting licences and then making businesses wait for the security nod, stretching over years, signifies an adverse regulatory environment. This is especially true when the government wants to intensify its reform trajectory, enabling ease of business and enhancing flow of foreign investments. To help realise the goals of satellite communications, the government departments and agencies must act in sync with one another rather than as individual power centres working in silos. While the licence — GMPCS — came from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), other approvals for satcom are granted by the Department of Space (DoS), Ministry of Home Affairs, and security agencies. In the case of Starlink, it’s been under scrutiny over its alleged role in the Russia-Ukraine war through its communication network.  While the security checks have to be foolproof, the government must provide clarity on the process of approvals and indicate a timeline for starting operations. Some of the satellites engaged for the yet-to-be launched satcom services are fast approaching end of life, having been on hold for so many years. Besides security approvals, there are other deliverables as well. For instance, the Union Cabinet has to give the final go ahead on spectrum pricing. More than a month ago, the Digital Communications Commission (DCC) — the highest decision-making body of the DoT — set satellite-spectrum pricing at 5 per cent of the adjusted gross revenue (AGR) of a telecom company. For services offered to remote and rural areas, there’s a discounted price, at 4 per cent of AGR. This followed a long-drawn dispute over the mode of spectrum allocation for satellite communication. The DCC decision, based on the recommendations of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai), will have to be taken up by the Union Cabinet. India’s satcom journey, expected to benefit low-connectivity areas including rural and hilly regions, should not face any more hurdles.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Satellite telecom sector in India Internet

entry.title: Institutional stability
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Institutional stabilityInstitutional stability

India needs timely appointments in higher education

premium

Prolonged vacancies in top academic positions raise concerns over faculty recruitment, research and institutional planning

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTSome of India’s premier higher-education institutions are facing a leadership vacuum, with 37 of the 155 Institutions of National Importance (23.9 per cent) operating under interim, acting or in-charge heads, additional-charge arrangements or extensions, according to a recent Hindustan Times analysis. The problem is particularly acute in central universities, where 20 of 48 institutions analysed have an interim leadership or extended tenures. Some vacancies persist despite posts being advertised months or even years earlier. This is more than an administrative inconvenience. Vice-chancellors and directors oversee faculty recruitment, academic programmes, budgets, infrastructure, and research partnerships. Prolonged uncertainty can delay decisions on new courses, the setting up of laboratories, and long-term financial commitments. Interim heads may also be reluctant to undertake major reforms when their authority is temporary. Additional-charge arrangements compound the problem by dividing the attention of senior academics between institutions. Hence, prolonged vacancies can put institutions in “standby mode”, weakening accountability and long-term planning.  The consequences are serious because leadership gaps coincide with wider capacity constraints in higher education. According to an analysis by PRS Legislative Research, 29 per cent of the sanctioned teaching posts in central universities were vacant as of December 2024. For professors, the vacancy rate stood at 56 per cent. These shortages place additional pressure on existing faculty. The appointment process also needs closer scrutiny. The analysis highlights cases in which selection procedures had begun well before the incumbent’s tenure ended, yet successors were not announced in time. Indira Gandhi National Tribal University, for instance, had functioned without a regular vice-chancellor for nearly 21 months, although the post had been advertised in June 2024 and re-advertised in March 2026. Such delays raise questions about administrative efficiency. Disputes over search committees and compliance with selection norms can further erode confidence in the process. Transparent, merit-based appointments are essential to protecting institutional credibility and autonomy.  The government should begin selection at least six months before a vacancy arises. It should establish binding timelines for screening applications, convening search committees and announcing appointments, with periodic public updates on progress. Such reporting would make delays visible and strengthen oversight without giving the government greater control over academic decisions. Committees should have clear selection criteria, independent members and safeguards against arbitrary interference. Interim appointments must be strictly time-bound, with extensions permitted only in exceptional circumstances and accompanied by a clear explanation. Institutions could also have contingency plans to ensure that essential academic and financial decisions continue during transitions. Strengthening leadership continuity and institutional autonomy is essential to improving research, teaching quality, and India’s global competitiveness in higher education. Timely leadership appointments are a basic requirement for that task. Leadership gaps and an inadequate strength of teaching staff, even in India’s premier institutions, could seriously undermine the country’s broader objective of achieving higher sustainable growth and becoming a developed country by 2047.     Topics : higher education vacancies governance Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Improved closing auction
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Improved closing auctionImproved closing auction

Sebi should aim to increase participation

premium

Securities and Exchange Board of India | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:13 PM ISTIt has been 10 weeks since the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) changed the way the stock markets end their trading day. It introduced the closing auction session (CAS) on August 3, with the idea of giving one efficient price for index funds, large institutional investors, and derivatives traders. But, instead, it led to problems — especially for derivatives traders, who decided to stay out of the market because of the unpredictability and volatility during the end session. A new circular dated October 15 addresses the issues and is in the right direction. It has delinked derivatives from the CAS close. The notional average daily derivatives turnover is more than 200 times that in cash. Retail investors account for about 40 per cent of the turnover in index options. The CAS was putting all these traders out of the system. The problems should be fixed in December.  The issue started when the indicative equilibrium prices in the CAS system fluctuated wildly as algo traders entered and cancelled orders, which led to volatility. The CAS settlement price is directly tied to expiring derivatives contracts, where traders had limited visibility of how the market would move. Thus, most derivatives traders and domestic funds stayed away from the market during the auction window. The bigger issue was that cash trading stopped at 3.15 pm while derivatives traded till 3.40 pm. The final value for the benchmark indices that came after the CAS was many a time far away from the closing price at 3.15 pm. Likewise for stocks that are part of the derivatives, or futures & options (F&O), segment.  The volumes handled in the auction are about 1 per cent of the daily cash turnover. The auction filled well on days when indices were rebalanced. For example, on the day of MSCI rebalance there were many buyers and sellers in the auction session and volumes were at 22 per cent of the entire trading day. But in normal days it lacked participants and sufficient volumes. In comparison, on the New York Stock Exchange, the CAS handles 12.43 per cent of daily volumes, and the same is 10 per cent for the Nasdaq. In such markets, it is hard for any single player to move the closing price because the CAS accounts for more than 10 per cent of the volumes. In India, the volumes are only 1 per cent and a small player can move stocks and thereby the index in the auction session and make money out of derivatives trades.  The new circular addresses most of these issues. From December 7, the expiry session goes back to the previous 25-year-old system of volume weighted average price (VWAP) while the daily closing price of underlying stocks will continue to be determined via CAS. Expiring index derivatives will stop trading at 3.30 pm or the same time as the cash markets. The auction will happen afterwards (3.30-3.40 pm) but stock derivatives will continue to trade until 3.45 pm.  This is a return to the old system but the auction stays and sets the official closing prices. But the link between derivatives and VWAP is restored. However, Sebi is yet to address how to bring in more passive funds to participate, improve the securities lending and borrowing mechanism (SLBM) or short selling, or separate auction order types that exist in the developed markets. A working stock-lending and short-selling market would let traders sell borrowed shares in an auction where buyers are bigger in numbers, narrowing the imbalances at the close. Thus, there is more to be done. Most importantly, fix stock lending and deepen the auction pool.     Topics : SEBI Indian stock market derivatives trading Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

Personal details can make fraud more convincing, while AI tools can exploit familiar security weaknesses at speed and scale. The editorial calls for prompt customer notification when material data exposure is credibly suspected, alongside enforceable standards for API, cloud, third-party and AI-agent security. Delhi’s early move to invoke the first stage of Grap is a welcome but untested response to worsening air quality. Its impact will depend on enforcement, weather and seasonal sources such as stubble burning and fireworks. Neighbouring cities and rural districts also need coordinated measures, with the National Capital Region Planning Board helping align urban action. Without this wider effort, city-level plans will remain largely ineffective, says today’s second editorial.  Despite a 12.6 per cent monsoon rainfall deficit and a super El Niño, kharif sowing area fell just 1.2 per cent in 2026, but Nikhil Gupta cautions against interpreting this as evidence of limited economic damage. Historical data show that yields and agricultural output typically fall sharply during El Niño years, with the effects concentrated in the second half. Gupta expects agricultural GVA growth to slow to 1.4 per cent in FY27 from 3 per cent in FY26, alongside weaker rural wages and consumption. Including fiscal constraints, inflation and base effects, he expects overall GVA and GDP growth to fall below 6 per cent in the second half. The European Union’s tightening steel import rules reflects a broader shift from tariff barriers to complex regulatory requirements covering emissions, sustainability, traceability and supply chains. Sangeeth Selvaraju and Prachi Priya argue that measures such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and corporate sustainability rules are raising compliance costs for exporters, even where free-trade agreements eliminate tariffs. Restrictions on waste shipments could also limit access to recycled raw materials outside Europe. For India, the authors recommend inter-ministerial coordination, a regulatory help desk under the India-EU FTA, systematic tracking of compliance costs and coalitions with developing countries. Industry must also invest in traceability, emissions measurement and shared compliance support for smaller firms. Nivedita Mookerji reviews Anil Sasi’s The EV Evolution: Then, Now and Next of Electric Vehicles, which examines India’s electric mobility transition through the lens of public policy, industrial history and technological choices. Sasi contrasts India’s shifting, often ad hoc approach with China’s sustained support for its domestic EV industry, highlighting how early pioneer Reva lost ground despite entering the market well before Tesla. The book traces government incentives, charging infrastructure costs and consumer concerns, while arguing that hybrids could provide an interim route to electrification. Though India’s EV ambitions are clear, Mookerji notes, the book leaves the central question unresolved: what is the country’s concrete roadmap to an electric future?

entry.title: Are works of fiction really all fiction?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Are works of fiction really all fiction?Are works of fiction really all fiction?

Fiction offers more than entertainment, opening windows to new worlds, building knowledge and keeping the reading habit alive amid digital distractions

premium

Books by Arthur Hailey, for instance, used to be so well researched that each of them gave a young reader a window to a new world

Ambi Parameswaran6 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 12:11 AM ISTThe news item about the passing away of the British writer Jeffrey Archer caught my attention (October 7, Business Standard). It also reminded me of the many occasions where I got to listen to him, in Mumbai and Jaipur. His books have sold millions of copies in India and I am told he wanted his books to hit the bookshops in India early to scupper the plans of pirated copy makers.  Jeffery Archer, with others like John Grisham and Dan Brown, brought back young people into reading English fiction. In order to understand the changing habits of youngsters with respect to popular culture, I usually do a survey among my students at the S P Jain Institute of Management and Research: What they read (fiction/ non-fiction); what they watch; what they listen to etc.  What surprises me is the range of fiction books they read. Some of them mention Harry Potter to be the last fiction book they have read.  That aside, I see Dan Brown, Jeffrey Archer, John Grisham, Amitava Ghosh, Amish, Chetan Bhagat. I also see books like The Kite Runner, Kafka on the Shore; even some old classics like Animal Farm and Brothers Karmazov. In a class of 80, I often get at least 50 distinct names mentioned. Very few get multiple mentions.  I wonder — if someone had done a similar survey in the late 1970s or ’80s, would we have got such divergent choice of books? Remember the question is very specific: Which is the last fiction book you have read?  We keep hearing that the book reading habit is dying. Bookshops are shutting down. Physical books are on their way out. A lot of that is true. There is just a lot more content out there. In the form of social media posts and Insta reels. The fight for consumer attention has never been more fierce. It is only getting more intense with AI Slop ruling the waves.  The signs are everywhere. As a school student, in the 1970s, growing up in Chennai, I was a regular at all the local libraries — the Central Library, the British Council Library, etc. But my favourite was the Easwari Lending Library. It started as an old paper mart but became a library that kids and elders used to throng.  A few years ago I had the opportunity to spend some time at the very same library. It is now being run by the founder Palani’s son. They still have a great collection. And have multiple branches across Chennai including dedicated libraries in gated communities. But I was told that except for the weekends, they don’t have the kind of crowds they used to have a few decades ago. While they have several thousand members, most of them don’t visit too often. Even when they come, they don’t borrow too many books. One other interesting trivia that he shared was that with kids, there is often a reading wave. Some authors will trend for a few years. Only to fade away. Unlike the B School students we saw, school students seem to be reading fiction books in groups. So if you did the same survey among 80 school students in say Class 9 you may get only 10 titles as the last fiction book read.  Why does reading fiction matter? Even for a business school student?  I remember a business leader, the CEO of a large company, a voracious reader no less, who introduced me to the book On War by Carl von Clausewitz, telling me proudly that he never read fiction. I did not want to tell him why he should start reading fiction but I got an answer in a talk that author Amitav Ghosh gave a few years ago at one of his book launches. He said that when Leo Tolstoy was writing his magnum opus War and Peace he thought he was writing history. It turned out to be, what we call, historical fiction. In a similar vein, Amitav Ghosh explained, his series of books, The Ibis Trilogy, are deeply researched to the extent they are historically accurate, but are fiction all the same.  Books by Arthur Hailey, for instance, used to be so well researched that each of them gave a young reader a window to a new world. The world of hospitals, or airports for instance.  Reading books by Jeffrey Archer gave us a window to the world of British politics, banking, nobility and more. John Grisham gave us a window to the world of law. Then there are those books that are sheer reading pleasure and nostalgia. You can put R K Narayan at the top of that list.  How to find the time to dive into fiction in our busy busy world? Some friends of mine have gone fully audio. They use their morning walk to listen to a book. Some others have opted for the digital version of books, sampling them on their ride home. I am sure if you see value you will find the time. In my mind it is a misnomer to classify all works of fiction as just time-pass. Let me share an interesting incident about books. Fiction.  I was on a flight back from Kochi to Mumbai. I had the latest Tom Clancy book for company and was immersed in it. Next to me was a smart young person who was observing me keenly. After a bit, he asked me: Do you read these heavy Tom Clancy books? I told him I do and I find them unputdownable. And greatly educative. To that he said he was with the Indian Navy and with the Southern Naval Command based in Kochi. It is a major operational and training hub. He told me that Tom Clancy’s books were recommended reading for every trainee.  We then got into an interesting discussion about how much research must have gone into even fiction books. By the time I landed in Mumbai my belief in reading fiction was further strengthened.
The writer is a best-selling author of books on brands, consumers and advertising. He is also an independent brand coach      Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. Today's editorials and columns examine delays in satellite broadband approvals, highway construction safety, India's role in WTO reforms, the RBI's rupee strategy and the struggle for women's rights

WTO, World Trade Organization(Photo: Shutterstock)

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  India’s satellite broadband rollout is being held back by regulatory delays, despite licences granted to Starlink, Jio Satellite and Eutelsat OneWeb. Our first editorial says that prolonged security clearances, involving multiple government departments and agencies, create uncertainty and undermine the country’s ease-of-business and investment goals. While security checks must be rigorous, authorities should clarify approval procedures and timelines. The Union Cabinet must also approve satellite spectrum pricing, following the Digital Communications Commission’s recommendation of 5 per cent of adjusted gross revenue, with a lower rate for rural services. Better coordination is essential to bring connectivity to underserved regions without further delays.  The government’s plan to penalise road contractors for fatal accidents caused by construction deficiencies is a step towards accountability, but today's second editorial argues that punishment after a tragedy is insufficient. Contractors face an opportunity to rectify defects, with fines for repeat accidents, yet stronger project appraisal, engineering oversight and independent inspections are needed to prevent flaws in the first place. India recorded over 183,000 road deaths in 2025, highlighting the urgency. Existing contracts already provide for quality checks and defect-liability periods. The government must therefore examine why these safeguards fail, particularly on national highways, where construction quality has life-or-death consequences. Dammu Ravi makes the point that India should lead WTO reform by balancing emerging economies’ responsibilities with poorer countries’ needs. While global trade grew 4.2 per cent in 2025, unilateral tariffs and weakening multilateral rules threaten developing nations. India could voluntarily reduce some special concessions, shift farm support towards direct income transfers, and replace capacity-enhancing fisheries subsidies with targeted assistance. Ravi also urges reform of consensus-based decision-making, greater engagement in plurilateral negotiations, and restoration of the WTO’s dispute settlement mechanism. With its economic weight and negotiating experience, India can help build a more inclusive trading system and strengthen the Global South’s collective influence. The RBI’s aggressive intervention to stabilise the rupee risks depleting foreign exchange buffers without addressing underlying weaknesses, cautions Rajesh Kumar. Although FCNR(B) deposits helped mobilise $133 billion, India’s external vulnerability stems less from its current account deficit than insufficient capital inflows. Foreign investors have withdrawn over $26 billion from Indian financial assets in 2026, amid competition from artificial intelligence investments and attractive yields on developed-market bonds. Kumar warns that an AI-market correction could intensify global financial instability and capital flight. India must adjust domestic policies to changing global conditions rather than rely on currency intervention or hope for renewed inflows. Akankshya Abismruta reviews Mihira Sood’s Courting Equality, which traces India’s women’s rights movement through landmark legal cases, political shifts and public protests. Sood examines how feminist activism brought violence against women into the public domain, challenged institutional impunity and shaped laws on rape and workplace harassment. The book also explores the Hindu Right’s appropriation of women’s rights issues and tensions between generations over legal remedies and #MeToo solidarity. Though some chapters are uneven and older cases may lose readers, Abismruta finds the work an illuminating account of a legal system that continues to deny women agency, while offering a framework for resistance.

entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished awayBest of Opinion: Trade-offs should be made visible, not wished away

Today's editorials and columns examine the trade-offs shaping India's economic policies, from China trade and poverty reduction to rupee management and the hidden costs of clean energy

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTPolicy choices rarely come without a bill. Opening markets can increase opportunity but also exposure. Reducing poverty may leave the hardest pockets of deprivation behind. Supporting one macroeconomic objective can make another harder to achieve. Defending a currency may buy stability while creating distortions elsewhere. Even clean energy carries environmental and geopolitical costs. The difficult part of policymaking is not finding benefits; it is deciding which costs are worth bearing, who should bear them, and how they can be contained. Our first editorial today, “Dropping barriers”, looks at India’s economic engagement with China. New Delhi has reason to seek better access to Chinese markets and press Beijing to dismantle tariff and non-tariff barriers that disadvantage Indian exporters. Greater access could help narrow the trade imbalance and create opportunities for Indian firms. But closer engagement cannot ignore strategic vulnerability or the competitive pressure created by China’s industrial strength. India must therefore pursue market access without allowing economic dependence to deepen. Openness can create gains, but only if it is accompanied by stronger domestic competitiveness and a clear-eyed assessment of risk. The second editorial, “Sustaining progress”, turns to poverty reduction. World Bank estimates suggest India has made significant progress, but aggregate improvement can obscure those who remain difficult to reach. Poverty is increasingly concentrated in certain states, regions and social groups, while employment quality and income security remain critical. The next stage is harder than the last. Sustaining the gains will require more jobs, better targeting and sharper attention to areas that have not benefited equally from growth. Ananth Narayan’s column, “Confronting economic trade-offs”, makes the theme more explicit. Monetary and financial policy involves objectives that can pull in different directions. Interest rates, liquidity, inflation, the exchange rate, fiscal conditions and capital flows cannot all be optimised independently. A measure that eases one pressure can intensify another. The challenge for policymakers is not to eliminate trade-offs, which is impossible, but to acknowledge them, rank priorities and communicate those choices clearly. Rajeswari Sengupta’s column, “RBI’s rupee fix: What is it solving?”, asks whether recent efforts to support the rupee are aimed at the right problem. Measures that ease immediate pressure on the currency may provide temporary stability, but they cannot substitute for stronger underlying capital flows and external-sector fundamentals. If the diagnosis is wrong, the cure can impose new costs without resolving the original weakness. “Dirty truths behind clean energy”, Prosenjit Datta’s review of Nicolas Niarchos’ The Elements of Power, exposes the trade-offs embedded in the energy transition itself. Batteries, solar equipment and electric vehicles promise lower carbon emissions, but depend on large-scale extraction of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other minerals, creating environmental, social and geopolitical risks of their own. There are few costless choices, these pieces reveal. Good policy begins when the trade-offs are made visible rather than wished away.
